items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: But I remember him well because he was a close friend, and sometimes my father and he would take me to — well they were soccer fans and would go to soccer games.

ctx.x: Oh yes. I understood that. I mean I didn’t understand it on a very highly sophisticated level, but I absolutely knew — we still didn’t know at that time — that was before the Holocaust really, it was before — 1942 was really when that really evil stuff — but it was bad enough as it was. I remember even before, when I was about six or so, one of my aunts had a boyfriend who was — this was at my grandmother’s place — and like

everybody of a certain age there, he was forced into doing stuff for the government. And he was actually in a kind of labor gang, not full time, but they were working on building the famous Autobahn. And he had to wear a kind of uniform thing with a swastika armband. And I remember him arriving at my grandmother’s and tearing off this thing and throwing it in a corner and saying, you know, as if it was something dirty. He left very soon after. He wanted my aunt to come with him. He went to Australia. He…
Can I ask you about a word you used when you were describing your father’s family, they were religious, and you used a word — Hasidm?

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I was very fond of Berg, because he was always nice to me

ctx.x: My grandmother had bought a – she’s the one. Kleenow didn’t have any money. She had money. She came from a wealthy family. She had bought a place in the country that was near the Austrian border in Bavaria. It was an old, beautiful, large house that was – living quarters, and it also had an adjoining stable and a barn where you could – what they did in those days – you could process – harvest stuff. It had quite a bit of land attached to it. She built another house there, a smaller house, for the kids. There was…

the Nazis were taking over all these bureaucratic positions and didn’t know anything, so she managed to talk them into giving her a Danish passport. The Danish consulate was cooperative, I guess. She dumped me at my grandmother’s place and went to Denmark and prepared things there. Then my grandmother, who was a Danish national by marriage and was free to travel – this is still ’38. Things are not as they became later with closed borders. So we were able to get in Denmark. That was the last time that I saw my…

Anyway, Berg gave me this thing. I really liked it. Then two months later exactly, almost to the day, he was dead. My parents were very upset about this. So I remember that as my first experience with someone close having died. In Vienna my parents – they used to have these things like they have in most civilized times – they have concerts for young kids. So I would be taken to symphony concerts on a Sunday at noon or something like that. I remember I didn’t like the conductor. He was heavy-set, his tuxedo didn’t…
